title: Salem Witch Trials: 20 Executed; Spectral Evidence Controversy
description: The Salem witch trials of 1692 resulted in the execution of twenty people — nineteen by hanging and one (Giles Corey) by pressing with stones — and the imprisonment of over 150 in the Salem Village area of Massachusetts Bay Colony. Beginning with fits among girls in the household of minister Samuel Parris, the crisis escalated through the spring and summer with mass accusation driven partly by 'spectral evidence' (testimony that the accused's spirit had appeared in dreams or visions). The controversy over spectral evidence — whether the devil could assume the form of an innocent person — was central to the crisis; Increase Mather's Cases of Conscience (1693) arguing against spectral evidence helped end the prosecutions. The trials ended in autumn 1692 when Governor Phips dissolved the special court.
historiographical_note: Salem has generated an enormous historiography. Paul Boyer and Stephen Nissenbaum's Salem Possessed (1974) offered a social-economic interpretation focused on village factionalism. Mary Beth Norton's In the Devil's Snare (2002) emphasized the context of frontier warfare with Native Americans. John Demos's Entertaining Satan (1982) provided a psychological/anthropological approach. The trials' cultural significance in American consciousness far exceeds their scale compared to European persecutions.
source_method: Salem court records; Boyer and Nissenbaum, Salem Possessed (1974); Norton, In the Devil's Snare (2002); secondary scholarship
